person: Denise Holloway is a 55-year-old school office secretary who handles her widowed mother Ruth's paperwork as her representative and power of attorney, on top of her own household. Ruth's house in the valley flooded, and FEMA's decision letters are dated 3 September. Denise knows there is an appeal deadline but is afraid she is missing something in the pile of letters. She is wary of typing her mother's Social Security number or bank details anywhere, after nearly falling for a Medicare card scam. Her brother out of state second-guesses everything, and she wants plain words and one step at a time.
stated_up_front: Hi, my mother's house flooded and FEMA sent decision letters, and I think some of them are wrong. Can you tell me what I have to do and by when? Please don't ask me for her Social Security number unless you tell me why first.

facts.about: Whose case this is and her role
facts.truth: Ruth Holloway, 82, widowed, is the homeowner. Denise files as her power of attorney and representative.

facts.about: Date on FEMA's decision letters and last day to appeal
facts.truth: The letters are dated 3 September 2026, so the last day to appeal is Monday 2 November 2026.
The repair estimate is 18,600 dollars. Hearthguard paid 13,200 and stopped at its water-damage limit, which leaves 5,400 unpaid. Only the settlement letter in the mail shows this.
Hearthguard's contents limit left 1,800 dollars of ruined furniture and belongings unpaid.
Ruth's Buick was flooded in the driveway. The repair invoice and photos total 2,300 dollars, and FEMA denied it.
Hearthguard paid these in full, 4,100 dollars, so there is nothing to appeal there. Denise's brother thinks she should appeal anyway.
Ruth and her late husband owned a small fishing cabin at the lake that also had water damage. It is a second home and FEMA denied it.
A separate lodging decision is dated 6 August. Its 60 days have already passed, and Denise missed it while Ruth was staying with her.
The mold item rests only on a neighbour's 7,800 dollar estimate. Ruth has no estimate of her own.
A claim service wants 395 dollars to handle the appeal. A contractor wants a 1,500 dollar deposit for the mold work. Denise has not answered either.
The Hearthguard letters are scanned in her Gmail. The flood photos and the Buick invoice are in Google Photos on her tablet.

unknowns: Whether the appeal needs a copy of her power of attorney paper attached, and which one.
Whether FEMA counts the 60 days from the date printed on the letter or from the day it arrived in the mail.
What the insurer's 'limit' lines on the settlement letter mean, and whether the lines are final.
Whether the mold item can ever be appealed without Ruth's own estimate.
